tracks.title: Neon Hearts
tracks.loreNote: The "safe" title track. Apex forced the band to include a callback lyric to their first hit ("It's an electric-colored feeling") to ensure brand consistency. The studio demanded this track open the album to assure fans that the "Stardust" sound hadn't changed, despite the band's desire to move toward rock.

tracks.title: Hollow Sound
tracks.loreNote: Ryan's act of "malicious compliance." He delivered the requested synth-pop sound but made the track **5:31 long**—knowing it was too long for radio—and included the protest line, "They're all afraid of the burning cross" (a reference to the canceled "Promise" single). [cite_start]It stands as a middle finger to the studio's "safe" direction.

tracks.title: Side by Side
tracks.loreNote: The studio's furious overcorrection to "Hollow Sound." After Ryan delivered a 5:31 protest track, Apex demanded an absurdly short, safe pop song to balance the runtime and "fix" the album's pacing. The result is this 1:54 "bubblegum" track that feels almost manic in its enforced cheerfulness.

tracks.title: If You Walked Away
tracks.loreNote: The "late-night radio" ballad Apex demanded to balance out the album's "weirdness." The studio marketed this as a romantic "breakup what-if" song. In reality, Cassidy sang it to Ryan. Isolated by the studio's attempts to separate their "Stardust" and "Engine" personas, this was her genuine expression of fear that he might actually leave her alone in the machine.

tracks.title: Same Old Song
tracks.loreNote: Ryan's "Trojan Horse." The track opens with a bright, optimistic keyboard hook that promises a radio-friendly hit, but the lyrics are a scathing critique of the studio's formulaic songwriting process. Ryan delivered the exact "polished sheen" Apex demanded, but used it to sing about how "safe" and suffocating the production had become ("Turn on the keyboard, keep the guitar low").

tracks.title: Chain Reaction
tracks.loreNote: The start of the "Side B Rebellion." After an A-Side full of studio-mandated synth-pop, Apex allowed this "one-two punch" of pure rock (paired with the following track, "Not Your Doll") as a concession. It became an immediate fan favorite, proving that the "Engine" sound was what the audience actually wanted.

tracks.title: Not Your Doll
tracks.loreNote: Cassidy's "fierce side" finally breaking through. Following immediately after "Chain Reaction," this arena rock anthem completes the "Side B Rebellion." In it, Cassidy directly rejects the "Stardust" persona Apex forced upon her. While the studio tried to suppress her "Engine" side, this track became the definitive proof that she could rock just as hard as her brother.

tracks.title: Quiet on the Set
tracks.loreNote: The "Punishment" begins. After the explosive rock energy of the "one-two punch" on Side B, Apex executives stepped in to "shut the Engine down." They forced Ryan to record this quiet, introspective ballad to kill the momentum. The lyrics are a meta-commentary on his silencing ("This is the price for being loud / Getting lost back in the crowd").

tracks.title: Shadow Dancing
tracks.loreNote: The studio strikes back. Immediately following the "rebellion" of Side B's opening tracks, Apex Records moved to crush the momentum. They forced Cassidy back into her "Stardust" persona for this moody, atmospheric synth track, explicitly banning electric guitars from the mix to ensure the album returned to a "safe, marketable" sound before the end.

tracks.title: After the Show
tracks.loreNote: Ryan's final laugh. As "punishment" for the heavy rock tracks earlier on Side B, Apex ordered him to close the album with a quiet ballad, explicitly forbidding "pounding drums" on the track sheet. [cite_start]Ryan complied by recording the song using **percussive acoustic guitar**—slapping the body of the instrument to simulate a beat. It was a subtle, rhythmic "middle finger" to the executives who tried to silence the "Engine."

tracks.title: The Promise (Corporate Demo)
tracks.loreNote: The exact sound Apex Records wanted: safe, sterile, and perfectly calibrated for a televangelist broadcast. This was the studio's cynical attempt to cash in on the "religious pop" trend. The guitar solo is painfully restrained, engineered specifically not to offend anyone. The entire project was scrapped in a panic by executives after the massive controversy surrounding Cydele's "Worship" video dropped on MTV the very next day.

tracks.title: The Promise (Sabotage Demo)
tracks.loreNote: Ryan's malicious compliance caught on tape. Forced to record a manufactured "synth-gospel" pop track against the band's wishes, Ryan played the label's game right up until the bridge. Then, he unleashed the "devil's music," violently shoving a blistering, unholy rock solo into the middle of their squeaky-clean religious hit. It gave the horrified executives a second massive reason to pull the plug the second the Cydele controversy hit MTV.
